project_inclusion.source_count: see Master Plant Pool authoritative row
project_inclusion.range_basis: Native in Texas at state level, project 3-qualifying-county native proof still unresolved; cultivation is not a native county occurrence.

look_here_first: Find TERMINAL whorls of LONG narrow trumpet-shaped flowers, usually ~38–48 mm. The top pair of opposite leaves/bracts often FUSES into a round disk below the head. But this is also possible in white/Texas honeysuckle—measure the narrow elongated trumpet versus L. albiflora's short two-lipped flower.

morphology_keys.habit: Woody perennial twining or trailing vine with opposite simple oval to elliptic leaves; terminal upper pair often connate and perfoliate, bluish/glaucous underside possible.
morphology_keys.leaf_arrangement: Opposite simple leaves with entire to near-entire margins; petiole lengths and fused terminal bracts vary by species.
morphology_keys.flower: Showy cluster of long narrow tubular 5-lobed corollas in terminal whorls, often red/orange outside and yellow inside; tube is far longer relative to small lobes.
morphology_keys.fruit: Red-orange to scarlet berries; not unique among native comparison.
diagnostic_sequence: Follow the flower stalk to determine AXILLARY paired flowers versus TERMINAL whorls.
Check one lateral flower: short two-lipped (~17–20 mm) / long tubular (~38–48 mm) / long strongly two-lipped (~45–57 mm).
Examine whether fused terminal bracts occur; do NOT use fused bracts alone for native pair.
If berries are ripe, note red-or-orange vs black—but berries are supporting evidence.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Long mostly cylindrical 38–48 mm terminal trumpet flowers versus shorter white 17–20 mm clearly two-lipped L. albiflora; leaf fusion alone cannot decide. Against Japanese honeysuckle, terminal whorls versus axillary paired strongly bilabiate flowers; berries red not black. Trumpetvine Campsis has compound leaves and aerial rootlets.
